intro: Lewes is the county town of East Sussex, on the River Ouse below the South Downs. In Southover Grange Gardens, the public garden in the middle of town, a mulberry thought to be more than 350 years old sprawls inside its railings, its heavy limbs resting along the grass. A reader sent it to us with a photograph taken under a rainbow. The garden is free to walk into every day, and the tree is seen from the path.

trees.story:
Southover Grange Gardens in Lewes keep a mulberry that is thought to be more than 350 years old. That is the figure the Parks and Gardens record of the garden gives, and the reader who sent it to us repeats it. If it holds, the tree was already growing while Charles II was on the throne.

It is not a tidy tree. The reader's photograph, taken when it stood bare with a rainbow over it, shows a short, leaning trunk that breaks into heavy limbs, several of which have come down to rest along the grass, with a tangle of thin branches above all of it. Black railings run round the whole tree, and a sign asks people to keep off.

In the reader's words, it is a "beautiful old black mulberry tree believed to be around 350 years old." The records we found say only mulberry, so the page leaves the exact species open until someone with a leaf in hand can confirm it. It stands near the terrace by the Ainsworth Room, in a public garden in the middle of town that is free to walk into every day.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the black railings round it and the heavy limbs lying along the grass. It stands near the terrace by the Ainsworth Room in Southover Grange Gardens.

question_meta: The old mulberry in Southover Grange Gardens, Lewes: how old it is and where to find it.
question_answer: The mulberry in Southover Grange Gardens, Lewes, is thought to be more than 350 years old. It stands railed off near the terrace by the Ainsworth Room, in a public garden that is free to visit every day.
question_context: The Parks and Gardens record of Southover Grange gives the mulberry an age of more than 350 years, and the reader who sent it to us says the same. Nobody has published a ring count or a measurement. The reader calls it a black mulberry; the records name only a mulberry, so the species is left open. The tree leans and sprawls, and several heavy limbs have come down to rest along the grass inside black railings, with a sign asking people to keep off. It stands near the terrace by the Ainsworth Room. Southover Grange Gardens are the town's public garden, run by the district council and open daily from dawn till dusk. The garden lies beside Southover Grange, a house of the 1570s, and its internal walls have arches made from the stone of Lewes Priory. Among its other specimen trees is a very early tulip tree more than 18 metres tall, and the Winterbourne stream runs through it. The record gives the mulberry's age as around 350 years in one place and over 350 in another.

faq.q: How old is the Lewes mulberry?
faq.a: More than 350 years by the Parks and Gardens record of the garden; it has not been dated by a ring count.
Yes. Southover Grange Gardens are a free public garden open every day; the tree is railed off and seen from the path.
